newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan aims to become player in Siberia energy.
newsitem.headline: Japan aims to become player in Siberia energy.

text.p: Japan could become a major player in developing energy resources in eastern Siberia, a senior Japanese industry official told a seminar on Monday.

Although unfavourable conditions which are hindering investment in Russia, such as tax laws, do not differ between regions, investment in eastern Siberia is appealing to Japan for a number of reasons, said Satoshi Tono, vice president of the state-owned Japan National Oil Corp (JNOC).
In addition to the geographical vicinity to Japan, the area has great potential for further discoveries of oil and natural gas reserves, he said.
"Japan may become a major player in the region as priority (in developing energy resources) turns towards geographical factors," Tono said.

Japanese and Russian energy officials told the seminar, aimed at promoting investment in Russia's energy sector, that eastern Siberia is highly attractive to Japan's energy industry because of its geographical proximity.
"Eastern Siberia has the potential to become a supplier of energy resources to Asia," Tono said.

He said chances were high that Japanese firms could help speed up progress in plans for the development of the Kovyktinskoye gas field near Lake Baikal in Irkutsk, or a pipeline for project participants. Development of the field is being studied by Russia and Chinese firms, and South Korean firms are also keen to take part.
Anatolij Shatalov, first vice-minister at Russia's Fuel and Energy Ministry, said he also expected Japanese firms' interest to be focused on eastern Siberia.
"Investment in eastern Siberia would be most economic for Japan, and would work to strengthen ties between the two," he said.
Tono cautioned that further improvements were needed to lure Japanese investors to the region.

He cited as hindrances the unstable status of joint-venture projects, an inability to forecast income due to frequent changes to tax laws, restrictions on exports, foreign exchange rules and use of pipelines.
"We would like to see the production-sharing agreements contracts come into force, the economic profitability of joint-venture projects clarified and transport methods secured," he said.
Shatalov said he expected a law on production sharing to be ratified by parliament in the near future.
Both Japanese and Western investors have been reluctant to invest in Russia's vast energy resources because of myriad taxes and various Russian policies.
Some firms already involved in joint ventures in Russia have changed plans and scaled down their investments to minimum levels, Tono said.
Russia, which produces about 6.2 million barrels of oil per day and is the world's third-largest oil producer, is estimated to hold about five percent of the world's proven reserves.
Japan, heavily reliant on the Middle East for its oil and gas imports, is eager to diversify its suppliers. About 80 percent of its crude oil imports are from the Middle East.
